query: For eutectic high-entropy alloys intended for structural applications, what single intervention could simultaneously increase strength and ductility? Formulate one testable hypothesis specifying the intervention, its proposed mechanism, the expected improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, the conditions under which it should hold, prior evidence supporting it, and an experiment that could falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a single-step thermo-mechanical treatment—specifically, cryo-rolling followed by an optimized annealing heat treatment—will refine the inherited lamellar dual-phase (soft FCC/hard BCC) structure in eutectic high-entropy alloys, thereby simultaneously increasing both yield strength and ductility compared to the as-cast state.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast eutectic high-entropy alloy with a naturally occurring lamellar microstructure that contains a soft FCC phase interleaved with a hard BCC (or B2/intermetallic) phase.
generation.intervention: Subject the as-cast alloy to cryo-rolling to induce severe deformation and grain refinement, followed by a controlled annealing treatment to restore ductility and promote a heterogeneous ultrafine-grained duplex lamellar structure.
generation.conditions: Room-temperature mechanical testing under quasi-static conditions on alloys having compositions similar to AlCoCrFeNi2.1; processing parameters (strain, cryogenic temperature, and annealing temperature/time) optimized for eutectic HEAs.
generation.structural_mediator: A refined ultrafine-grained duplex lamellar structure with a high density of phase boundaries that act as barriers to dislocation motion and microcrack propagation.
generation.mechanism: The severe deformation during cryo-rolling creates a high dislocation density and refines the microstructure, while the subsequent annealing balances recovery with controlled phase coarsening. This generates a hierarchical microstructure that enhances strain hardening (via dislocation storage and microcrack arrest mechanisms) and distributes local stresses more evenly, concurrently boosting strength and ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the as-cast baseline, the processed alloy is expected to show a significant increase in yield strength (potentially a 20–50% improvement) while maintaining or modestly enhancing ductility, overcoming the traditional strength–ductility trade-off.
generation.baseline: As-cast eutectic high-entropy alloy, which typically exhibits a compromise between high strength and ductility due to a coarser lamellar structure and less effective load transfer at phase boundaries.
generation.boundary: This improvement is anticipated to be effective primarily in eutectic high-entropy alloys with a distinct dual-phase lamellar microstructure; alloys lacking a well-defined eutectic architecture may not exhibit the same balance of properties.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of the strength and ductility improvements and the optimal processing parameters (e.g., rolling reduction, cryogenic temperature specifics, annealing time/temperature) need to be determined experimentally.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of eutectic high-entropy alloy samples with identical compositions and as-cast microstructures. Apply the proposed cryo-rolling plus controlled annealing treatment to one set while leaving the other set as-cast. Perform a series of room-temperature tensile tests on both sets and characterize the resulting microstructures using electron microscopy.
measurements: Microstructural grain size and phase distribution via SEM/TEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the processed samples do not show at least a 20% increase in yield strength and no improvement (or a deterioration) in ductility compared to the as-cast baseline, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractThe NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 is a refractory multi-principal-element alloy with high strength and good ductility at room temperature. It is important for possible high-temperature applications to investigate the deformation mechanism of the NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 alloy at different temperatures using tensile tests. In this investigation, the tensile tests were conducted at room temperature to 1273 K on sheet materials fabricated by cold rolling combined with annealing treatments. At 473 K, the NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 alloy exhibited a high tensile ductility (12%). At a testing temperature range of 673~873 K, the ductility was reduced, but the yield strength remained above 800 MPa, which is rare in most other alloys. The TEM investigations revealed that a dislocation slip controlled the plastic deformation, and the degree of deformation was closely related to the dislocation density. The true stress–strain curves of the alloy under different deformation conditions were obtained by tensile deformation at different deformation temperatures (673~873 K) and strain rates (0.001~0.0005 s−1). Realizing improved strength–ductility synergy in eutectic alloys acting as in situ composite materials remains a challenge in conventional eutectic systems, which is why eutectic high-entropy alloys (EHEAs), a newly-emerging multi-principal-element eutectic category, may offer wider in situ composite possibilities. Here, we use an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA to engineer an ultrafine-grained duplex microstructure that deliberately inherits its composite lamellar nature by tailored thermo-mechanical processing to achieve property combinations which are not accessible to previously-reported reinforcement methodologies. The as-prepared samples exhibit hierarchically-structural heterogeneity due to phase decomposition, and the improved mechanical response during deformation is attributed to both a two-hierarchical constraint effect and a self-generated microcrack-arresting mechanism. This work provides a pathway for strengthening eutectic alloys and widens the design toolbox for high-performance materials based upon EHEAs. Although the HEAs with a single solid-solution phase have some advantages (e.g., higher melting points than the HEAs with multi-phases, higher strength for the HEAs with a single BCC phase, better ductility for the HEAs with a single FCC phase etc.), their good properties are usually accompanied by some disadvantages, which are fatal for technological applications. One is that the HEAs with a single solid-solution phase usually have inadequate liquidity, poor castability and hence considerable chemical inhomogeneity [,]. The other is that the HEAs with a single solid-solution phase could not achieve a balance between high strength and good ductility (e.g., the HEAs with a single FCC phase were ductile but not strong enough while the HEAs with a single BCC phase were adequately strong but at risk of brittleness [,,,]).
